Reference › Benchmarks

Benchmarks

Measured on an Apple M1 Max (osx-arm64), .NET 10.0, Release build, Pare 0.7.0, 2026-10-31.

Library speed

BenchmarkDotNet 0.15.8, one TypeStripper.Strip call per source, output to a reused buffer:

Input Mean MB/s Allocated
TypeScript 5.9.3 checker.ts (3.1 MB) 9.4 ms 333 0 B
Real-world corpus, 2,392 files (19.5 MB) 60.7 ms 269 0 B
(a = nested 1,000 deep 36.5 ms 0.2 333 B

Deep nesting is quadratic, as in TypeScript's own parser. Real code never reaches it.

On Windows 11 x64 (AMD Ryzen 7 7840HS, .NET SDK 10.0.402), the same benchmarks give 8.4 ms (373 MB/s) for checker.ts, 53.5 ms (311 MB/s) for the real-world corpus and 29.9 ms for the nested case, all allocating nothing.

Against other tools

The same 2,392 files (TypeScript's compiler, Vue, Hono, Deno std, Svelte, Zod at pinned commits) through other tools. Each tool's output is compared with Pare's byte for byte, then as an Acornima syntax tree without locations. Printers (esbuild, oxc, Deno) reprint literals, so the tree comparison ignores literal spelling, { a: a } versus { a } and void 0 versus undefined. For printers, a looser comparison also ignores imports (they drop unused ones) and a numeric suffix on names (they rename a shadowed x to x1). Deno is Deno's own transpiler (swc, as deno run uses it), read from its cache after deno cache --no-check.

Tool Same bytes Same tree Same but imports dropped or names renamed Differ Throughput Pare is
Pare 0.7.0 - - - - 263 MB/s -
Node 24.16 stripTypeScriptTypes 1,898 490 - 0 38 MB/s 6.9x faster
oxc-transform 0.154.0 13 2,375 0 0 81 MB/s 3.3x faster
ts-blank-space 0.9.0 1,967 420 - 1 27 MB/s 9.7x faster
esbuild 0.28.2 11 1,961 296 120 11 MB/s 23.3x faster
Deno 2.9.8 (swc) 11 2,326 51 0 - -
  • Same tree but not the same bytes: Node and ts-blank-space keep tabs and write UTF-8-width spaces for non-ASCII comment text, and Pare writes its semicolon fixes in a few places they leave blank.
  • ts-blank-space's one difference is a bug on its side: get!: T followed by another field on the next line becomes a getter, and its output does not parse. Pare had the same bug until this comparison found it.
  • Deno's 51: it drops imports whose names are unused, including import {} from "m", which still loads m (Pare keeps it, as verbatimModuleSyntax requires), and renames shadowed bindings.
  • esbuild's 120: it turns strings with line breaks into template literals and folds some expressions. None is a Pare error.
  • Four files are left out: their output does not parse for any stripper, because they import or re-export a type without type, which needs type information to remove.
  • Whole process over all files: the pare CLI (NativeAOT) 0.94 s, deno cache --no-check from a cold cache 1.2 s, one run each.

Throughput is the best of 5 passes in one run on a laptop and moves by 10 to 20 percent between runs. The BenchmarkDotNet numbers above are the steady ones.

Real-world check

scripts/run-std-tests.cs runs Deno's standard library test suite on Pare's output. It strips a copy of denoland/std (pinned commit, 1,600+ files) with the pare CLI in about 0.5 s, points the @std/* imports at the .js files, and runs deno test on each package's original *_test.ts and stripped *_test.js:

  • 38 of 42 packages give the same result (4,997 passing tests). 5,521 tests pass on Pare's output in all.
  • csv: one test compares Function.prototype.toString() with Deno's reprinted (n)=>n. A blanking stripper keeps (n ) => n.
  • testing: snapshot tests look for a snapshot file named after the .ts test file.
  • http: one test passes only on the .js copy, because the TypeScript copy sits under a dot directory (.corpus) that serveDir() refuses.
  • expect: not run. Pare rejects three of its files (parameter properties and a <T>x assertion, which generate runtime code), so expect.js is missing.

Failures common to both runs (cli, encoding, fmt, fs and others) come from the environment.

Reproduce

bash 
dotnet run scripts/get-bench-corpus.cs                       # ~25 MB into .corpus/realworld
npm --prefix tests/Extrode.Pare.Bench/compare ci --ignore-scripts
dotnet publish src/Extrode.Pare.Cli -c Release -r osx-arm64 -o tmp/aot
dotnet run -c Release --project tests/Extrode.Pare.Bench -- compare --passes 5
dotnet run -c Release --project tests/Extrode.Pare.Bench -- --filter '*'
dotnet run scripts/run-std-tests.cs            # or name packages: ... -- yaml semver

compare writes every tool's output under tmp/compare/ and the differences to tmp/compare/differences.tsv.
